headline: Billingsgate on the Building Moon: Bass Glued to Bait, Blues Filling the Gaps
subhead: Stripers are stacked tight to mackerel and bunker but still won't commit to a blitz — the building moon should change that soon.
body_markdown:
The Bay is carrying more bait right now than it has all summer, and that's both the good news and the reason the striper bite has stayed frustrating for a lot of boats this week. Mackerel schools are thick off Race Point, peanut bunker are working their way along Sandy Neck and into Barnstable Harbor, and every drift through the rip turns up marks on the sounder that look like a school bus stacked on bait. But the fish underneath them are still sluggish about actually feeding hard. Water out there is holding onto its late-summer warmth, and warm water this time of year tends to keep bass content to sit under the bait and pick rather than blow it up on top. That's exactly the pattern the fleet has been talking about at the ramps in P-town and Barnstable all week — plenty of fish, not much urgency.

That's going to change, and soon. The moon is building toward full on the 6th and 7th, and every year around here that's when the tide starts running harder and those loose bait schools get squeezed into tighter, more nervous balls. Once that happens, the switch usually flips fast. We flagged this exact setup last week — said the early tide stages would keep producing while everything built toward a bigger push — and that's held up almost to the hour. The best fish of the week have come in the first two hours of the ebb off Race Point and the top of the flood pushing onto Peaked Hill Bars, right when the current starts stacking bait against the structure.

Race Point remains the best bet for size. Boats working the rip on the last of the slack into the first stage of the ebb are getting bass into the 20s and 30s on live mackerel, drifted naturally off a 3-way rig with just enough weight to hold bottom in that washing-machine current. A few better fish — high 30s, one report of a fish pushing 40 — came off live bunker fished the same way, just fished a little deeper in the guts of the rip where the bigger fish like to sit out of the heaviest wash. Depth there runs 20 to 35 feet depending on where you catch the tide, and the fish are moving with the bait, not holding on a fixed piece of structure, so staying mobile on the drift matters more than anchoring up.

Peaked Hill Bars has been a tube-and-worm and umbrella rig show, worked slow on the troll through the sandy troughs in 15 to 25 feet. It's a slower bite than the rip but a more consistent one — fewer giants, more keeper-class fish in the mid-20s to low 30s, and it's been holding up through the middle of the day when Race Point goes quiet on the higher stages of the tide.

Bluefish have been the one thing you can count on without much thinking. Sandy Neck and the mouth of Barnstable Harbor have had steady blitz activity on peanut bunker, especially in the last two hours of daylight when the bait gets pushed up against the beach. Poppers and 1-ounce metal have both worked — the blues aren't picky right now, they're just showing up in numbers and staying aggressive, which tracks with what's been reported basin-wide this summer. Expect that to hold through Labor Day week as long as the bait stays put.

Fluke have thinned out the way they always do this time of year. Billingsgate Shoal and the flats off Barnstable are still giving up keeper fish, but the doormats that were around in July have mostly slid off toward deeper structure, and the numbers game just isn't what it was a month ago. If you're still chasing them, work the edges of the shoal on the drift with 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, and don't expect to grind through many shorts to find a keeper — the ratio has flipped.

Cod are still a step behind. The deeper structure north of Race Point and off the backside of Peaked Hill Bars — 90 to 130 feet — is starting to hold a few fish, but the water hasn't cooled enough yet to bring them up in real numbers. That bite typically builds through the rest of September and really turns on once the surface temps drop into the mid-50s. Worth a scout trip with diamond jigs if you're already out there, but it's not worth planning a whole day around yet.

Looking ahead, the next few days should keep rewarding the same pattern — early ebb and early flood at Race Point, midday on Peaked Hill Bars, dusk blitzes off Sandy Neck. If the moon does what moons do and tightens that bait up over the next week, look for the first real surface blitz activity to break loose right around the rip. Keep an eye on wind direction heading into the weekend — anything out of the northeast will stack more bait against Race Point and could be the trigger that turns this steady pick into the kind of push everyone's been waiting on.
